overview: The exact atlas id korea-usa is labeled “Korea (USA)” and indexed approximately from 1945 to 1960 as one state feature. That hybrid name is an editorial label, not a complete political identity. Its imported summary describes Korea across the peninsula, but the target geometry covers only a simplified southern shape. The MultiPolygon has 16 components, 16 rings, and 550 positions. Its bounds run from about 125.89 to 129.59 degrees east and 33.19 to 37.93 degrees north. Sampled Seoul, Busan, Gangneung, and Jeju are inside; Pyongyang, Wonsan, Ulleungdo, and Dokdo are outside. The boundary is also inconsistent with a simple 38th-parallel division. Kaesong and Haeju are assigned to a northern ussr feature labeled “Korea (USSR),” sampled Sokcho has no owner, and that northern feature reaches Dandong in China. The target shares one topology arc with that northern feature. The layer therefore looks like a later South-Korea-shaped polygon projected backward rather than a surveyed 1945 jurisdiction. At the 1960 snapshot, korea-usa disappears and korea-republic-of begins; the 1994 atlas record continues that southern state. This seam is continuity, not a fall or population replacement. The atlas supplies a time box and imperfect outline. The sections below use historical sources, rather than the label alone, to reconstruct changing governments and lives within it.

periods.title: 1945 to 1946: liberation, occupation, return, and shortage
periods.summary: Japanese rule ended, U.S. troops entered the southern zone, and military government claimed authority while refusing rival Korean governments. Return migration, disrupted production, hunger, and arguments over administration shaped daily life. Schools reopened quickly, but books, staff, food, and institutional decolonization remained uneven.

periods.title: 1946 to 1947: rice controls, protest, and fragile institutions
periods.summary: Military government reversed its early free-market rice policy, collected grain, and rationed cities amid shortages and black markets. Labor, peasant, rightist, and leftist conflict intensified. Public-health and education offices expanded ambitions while lacking staff, supplies, and broad trust; official plans cannot be read as equal results.

periods.title: 1947 to 1948: divided diplomacy, Jeju violence, and election
periods.summary: U.S.-Soviet negotiations remained deadlocked and the Korean question moved to the United Nations. A March 1947 police shooting and subsequent strike preceded escalating violence on Jeju. The May 1948 election occurred only where the UN commission had access, preparing a southern government under deep political division.

periods.title: 1948 to 1949: Republic founded and military government ended
periods.summary: The Constitution took effect and the Republic of Korea was inaugurated on 15 August 1948, ending U.S. military government. Jeju repression continued, the Yeosu-Suncheon revolt and suppression widened killing, and the security state hardened. A December aid agreement recast American support as relations between governments.

periods.title: 1949 to 1950: land reform, state consolidation, and exposed peace
periods.summary: Land-reform legislation followed earlier distribution of formerly Japanese-owned land, with implementation beginning in March 1950. Reform reduced landlord power but involved repayment, pre-sales, and wartime disruption. Political repression continued, while southern infrastructure and electricity remained vulnerable within a peninsula already divided into rival states.

periods.title: 1950 to 1951: invasion, flight, occupation changes, and survival
periods.summary: North Korean forces invaded in June 1950. Rapid advances, counteroffensives, and Chinese intervention shifted front lines repeatedly. Civilians fled by foot, rail, and ship; families separated; Busan and other southern places absorbed refugees. Military histories establish campaign sequence, while Korean and UN sources reveal displacement and relief conditions.

periods.title: 1951 to 1952: positional war, camps, tent schools, and relief
periods.summary: The front stabilized near the eventual armistice line while fighting and negotiations continued. Refugees, war sufferers, and destitute residents relied on unequal combinations of kin, work, markets, state offices, and international relief. Tent schools and camp medical and sanitation programs show organized responses without proving adequate reach or outcomes.

periods.title: 1952 to 1953: prolonged war, political crisis, and armistice
periods.summary: Battle and armistice talks continued through political conflict inside the Republic. Refugee return and resettlement remained dangerous and incomplete. The armistice signed in July 1953 halted open fighting and created a military line, but it was not a peace treaty; separated families and destroyed homes outlasted the ceasefire.

periods.title: 1953 to 1955: ceasefire, reconstruction, and persistent illness
periods.summary: Reconstruction repaired schools, hospitals, water systems, transport, and homes through Korean labor, public programs, foreign aid, and military assistance. Tuberculosis, weak nutrition, damaged infrastructure, and displacement constrained recovery. Records of facilities and deliveries prove organized programs, but they cannot by themselves demonstrate completion, access, or equal benefit.

periods.title: 1955 to 1960: reconstruction, radio, and the April Revolution
periods.summary: Authoritarian government and electoral manipulation provoked opposition as reconstruction continued. GoldStar launched the A-501 radio in 1959, a qualified domestic-manufacturing milestone. Student-led protest against the fraudulent March 1960 election broadened into the April Revolution, and Syngman Rhee announced his resignation on 26 April.

sections.title: Read the atlas label, border, government, and writing carefully

items.text: The exact id korea-usa is an atlas shorthand, not a country name, annexation, citizenship, or fifteen-year American government. The one indexed layer runs approximately from 1945 to 1960, while its imported peninsula-wide Korea summary is too broad for this southern geometry and mixed political interval.

The 1945 feature is a MultiPolygon with 16 components, 16 rings, 550 positions, and bounds of about 125.89 to 129.59 degrees east and 33.19 to 37.93 degrees north. Sampled Seoul, Busan, and Jeju are inside; Pyongyang, Wonsan, Ulleungdo, and Dokdo are outside.

The polygon is not the actual September 1945 occupation zone. Kaesong and Haeju, both south of 38 degrees north, are assigned to the northern ussr feature; sampled Sokcho has no owner; and that northern feature reaches Dandong in China. The atlas projects a later southern outline backward.

U.S. military government ended on 15 August 1948, although troop withdrawal, aid, alliance, and wartime command followed separate timelines. The Republic of Korea existed through the remaining atlas interval. Keeping those institutions distinct prevents the hybrid label from turning occupation, sovereignty, and American influence into synonyms.

Written sample from the enacted 1948 Constitution: “대한민국은 민주공화국이다.” Readable transliteration: “Daehan Minguk-eun minju gonghwaguk-ida.” Official English: “The Republic of Korea shall be a democratic republic.” This is formal state language, not every Korean person’s speech or consent, and constitutional promise cannot substitute for political reality.

sections.title: Occupation rule, Korean political projects, and the 1948 transfer

items.text: MacArthur’s proclamation asserted military authority south of the 38th parallel and made English the official language of military control. Korean committees, parties, officials, workers, farmers, and returning exiles did not simply wait for orders. The proclamation proves a claim of command, not public agreement or smooth local compliance.

Military government retained much of the colonial administrative apparatus, rejected the Korean People’s Republic and the Provisional Government as governments, and only gradually placed more Koreans in offices while Americans kept final power. “Koreanization” therefore describes staffing changes within occupation, not full self-government.

The 1945 U.S. directive called for restoring utilities, maximizing food, reopening schools, protecting archives, supervising parties, censoring communications, and controlling former Japanese assets. It reveals occupation priorities and powers. A directive records what officials were told to pursue, not what every village received or how Koreans judged it.

A 1947 U.S. policy memorandum acknowledged deep antagonism, riots, economic strain, and the failure to secure a joint settlement with the Soviet Union. Its proposed relief and educational measures belong to American strategic reasoning. They should be read beside Korean conflict, not treated as a neutral diagnosis of society.

The May 1948 election was observed in the area accessible to the United Nations commission, not across the peninsula. State functions passed to the Republic after its August inauguration; remaining transfers and U.S. troop withdrawal were separate. This sequence created a southern state without resolving competing peninsula-wide claims.

sections.title: Founding, land, repression, elections, and democratic protest

items.text: The 1948 Constitution declared a democratic republic and established a legal order for the new state. A constitution is evidence of institutional design and claims to legitimacy. It does not prove that elections were fair, police power restrained, political opponents safe, or the rights printed in it equally experienced.

Jeju 4·3 grew from a March 1947 police shooting and strike before the armed uprising of 3 April 1948. Armed insurgents, police, rightist groups, soldiers, and state forces acted in an escalating conflict, and scorched-earth repression killed many civilians. Estimates and political labels require attribution rather than false precision.

At Yeosu in October 1948, members of the 14th Regiment refused orders to deploy against Jeju and revolted. Government suppression retook Yeosu and Suncheon amid extensive killing, including civilians. The incident fed stronger security law and anticommunist repression, while responsibility, labels, and casualty totals remain contested.

Land reform combined distribution of formerly Japanese-owned land with a 1949 law implemented from March 1950. It sharply weakened tenancy and landlord power, but repayment burdens, sales before implementation, and wartime disruption limited gains. The source supports a major change, not a single clean or universally beneficial event.

Students protested from February 1960; fraudulent voting on 15 March and police violence widened demonstrations to other students and civilians. Syngman Rhee announced his resignation on 26 April. The April Revolution is a political endpoint near the atlas seam, although the map’s id change was not caused by it.

sections.title: War, displacement, family separation, and the armistice

items.text: The Korean War began with the North Korean invasion in June 1950. Fronts moved rapidly south, then north, then south again before stabilizing near the later armistice line. Official U.S. Army histories establish campaign chronology, but their operational viewpoint cannot stand in for civilian memory, Korean politics, or atrocity history.

People escaped by walking, rail, road, or ship when routes existed. Some fled before armies, some were ordered to move, and some could not leave. Repeated occupation changes separated relatives and destroyed homes. Refugee is therefore a changing wartime condition, not one route, class, motive, or permanent identity.

Busan’s refugee population improvised shelter from boards, packing cases, cloth, and other salvaged materials when camps and housing were insufficient. Families queued for water and carried jars uphill. These concrete examples illuminate one pressured refuge city; they do not describe every displaced household or settlement.

United Nations reports organized recipients as refugees, war sufferers, locally destitute people, and people returning from camps. Those categories shaped relief delivery but could flatten family histories, disability, age, gender, and changing residence. Program totals and distributions document institutional action, not complete recipient experience or adequate provision.

The July 1953 armistice stopped open fighting and fixed a military separation line; it was not a peace treaty. Widowed people, orphans, disabled veterans and civilians, missing relatives, divided families, and displaced households faced different futures. The evidence supports enduring separation without turning every family into the same tragedy.

sections.title: Households, women, children, shelter, and daily adaptation

items.text: Liberation brought Koreans home from Japan and former imperial territories while division redirected movement across the peninsula. Returnees joined households already facing housing, food, and work shortages. Policy sources document population pressure more securely than private reunion, conflict, or care inside each family.

In wartime Busan, women sold porridge, noodles, and relief goods while men and women also sought hauling, dock, workshop, market, and casual labor. These documented survival strategies complicate a male-breadwinner picture. A teaching page supplies examples, not a workforce survey or proof of fixed gender roles.

A March 1946 Daegu report said about half of elementary pupils lacked lunch boxes, a local snapshot of urban hunger during rice shortage. It cannot establish a national child-hunger rate. Children’s access to meals depended on household grain, ration eligibility, markets, school, kin, aid, and place.

A 1954 Jeongneung project built 253 earth-brick homes as a reconstruction experiment. Such planned housing coexisted with rented rooms, repaired dwellings, shacks, camps, and rural homes. One project reveals materials and policy possibilities, not a typical house or evidence that displaced families obtained durable shelter.

Children learned, worked, played, queued, carried water, and cared for siblings under conditions that varied by household and safety. Archival photographs preserve particular moments of refuge and rebuilding. A photograph can show clothing, tools, posture, and place, but it cannot explain a child’s feelings without testimony.

sections.title: Schools, textbooks, tent classrooms, and student voices

items.text: Schools reopened in September and October 1945, often before a settled curriculum or adequate supply of teachers and books. Korean language and history returned after colonial suppression. Opening a school door did not guarantee attendance, meals, heat, materials, safety, or freedom from political direction.

Japanese imperial textbooks were removed, but replacements included hurried translations and provisional syllabi that retained some older structures. Curriculum revision therefore mixed decolonization, emergency improvisation, and institutional continuity. The documented national framework cannot show precisely what every teacher said or each child learned.

War closed or displaced many schools, yet classes continued in tents, borrowed rooms, and other improvised spaces. A later textbook synthesis confirms the institutional pattern, not the daily condition of every classroom. Weather, military danger, displacement, teacher availability, and family work all shaped whether children could attend.

The six-three-three structure and expanding institutions created a broader formal educational framework during the 1950s. This later synthesis does not measure who enrolled, stayed, advanced, or received comparable teaching across regions and wartime disruption. Questions about unequal access require household, school, and local records beyond this source.

Jin Yeong-suk, a second-year girls’ middle-school student, left a testament before joining an April 1960 demonstration against electoral fraud. Her writing makes one young participant’s decision visible. It must remain one individual voice, not a quotation placed in the mouths of all students, girls, or protesters.

sections.title: Food, farming, markets, labor, and material aid

items.text: Military government first loosened the rice market, then restored collection and rationing as shortage and prices worsened. Farmers faced compulsory deliveries, city residents queued, and black markets linked those pressures. Policy records describe rules and conflict; they do not reveal every harvest, meal, concealment, or exchange.

Official ration ceilings were not the same as grain actually received. Return migration, poverty, transport disruption, crop conditions, disease controls, household size, and market access all affected food. This rice-administration source establishes shortage and distribution conflict, but it does not reconstruct complete meals or diets across households and regions.

Land reform gave many cultivators a different relationship to their fields and reduced tenancy, while households still depended on labor, credit, seed, draft power, weather, prices, and repayment. War interrupted implementation. The reform belongs in daily-life history because ownership change did not remove the work or risk of farming.

At Busan’s docks and markets, refugees hauled cargo, carried loads, repaired goods, cooked, sold small portions of food, or traded relief items. Such work could sustain households while remaining irregular and insecure. These examples show livelihood improvisation around a port, not the national occupational structure.

The December 1948 aid agreement moved from occupation relief toward support negotiated between the United States and the Republic of Korea. Food, necessities, medicine, and other assistance entered political and commercial systems. Agreement and delivery records establish programs and flows; they do not show equal distribution, household use, or freedom from diversion and dependency.

sections.title: Medicine, public health, tuberculosis, and limits of care

items.text: Occupation authorities created a health bureau in 1945 and a larger welfare department in 1946, but trained personnel were scarce and the structure contracted in 1948. Later ministries were reorganized again. Administrative charts reveal responsibility and ambition; they cannot prove nearby clinics, affordable treatment, medicine, or public trust.

War, crowding, poor nutrition, disrupted transport, and damaged facilities intensified infectious-disease risks. Seoul planned BCG vaccination for residents under nineteen in 1950, but war interrupted the plan. The archive also notes later equipment and access gaps, so a vaccination proposal must not be reported as completed coverage.

A 1954 government estimate described widespread active tuberculosis, while hospital beds, X-ray equipment, trained staff, money, and continuing treatment were limited. Because the figure is an official estimate, it signals scale rather than a precise prevalence survey. Seoul evidence should not silently stand for every province.

By 1953, international aid supported a network of health centers and clinics, and later training sought to expand preventive care. These counts show facilities and programs, not whether each was continuously staffed, supplied, reachable, trusted, or effective. Home care, pharmacies, midwives, and other healers remained outside much official reporting.

A 1950 UN report described Korean medical teams, immunization, and environmental-sanitation work in refugee camps. That is evidence of organized emergency action. As an official wartime report, it cannot establish complete coverage, independent health outcomes, informed consent, or how camp residents experienced treatment and surveillance.

sections.title: Water, toilets, drains, waste, kitchens, and sanitation

items.text: Two institutional histories count either 79 or 83 cities with water systems in 1945. Their definitions and geographic bases are not reconciled, so this card preserves the conflict. Both agree that service reached a minority, war damaged systems, and household access varied sharply by city, neighborhood, and income.

The sewer museum reports national water-service coverage at about 17 percent in 1960, after wartime destruction and stalled recovery. A connection rate does not reveal water quality, reliability, affordability, household distance, or which non-network sources unconnected families used. It is an infrastructure measure, not a complete access history.

Refugees in hillside Busan settlements queued at scarce taps and carried heavy jars uphill. Women and children often performed water work, although roles differed among households. A local teaching account makes labor visible without proving one national pattern, an exact walking distance, or identical access in camps and villages.

War-damaged drains and sparse sewer investment left wastewater entering streams and spaces near homes. In Seoul, sewage from Cheonggyecheon shantytowns flowed untreated into the stream before covering work began in 1958. Drainage, wastewater removal, flood control, and drinking-water supply were related problems, not one interchangeable service.

No secure nationally representative survey in this packet establishes one household toilet type or a flush-toilet percentage for 1945 to 1960. Arrangements varied. A 1950 campaign mentioned latrines, waste, insects, bedding, and DDT, proving official sanitation pressure, not fixture design, safe chemicals, compliance, or equal facilities.

sections.title: Reconstruction, technology, archives, and the 1960 seam

items.text: Armed Forces Assistance to Korea records cover support for hospitals, schools, roads, water works, and other civic facilities after destruction. A records schedule proves the program and preserved series, not that every proposed project was finished or maintained. Korean labor, agencies, communities, and other aid systems also shaped rebuilding.

The United Nations Korean Reconstruction Agency coordinated relief and rebuilding after the invasion, while refugees and war sufferers also relied on Korean institutions, kin, markets, charities, and labor. UNHCR’s later retrospective establishes organizational context. It should be paired with contemporary Korean records rather than made the sole voice of recovery.

Fun fact: GoldStar launched the A-501 radio on 15 November 1959 and designed it to operate under poor low-voltage conditions. It was the first domestically produced Korean radio, although some components came from Japan. The milestone concerns manufacture and engineering, not immediate ownership or universal listening.

Archival photographs, official reports, laws, school texts, and military histories answer different questions. Photographs preserve selected scenes; reports preserve institutional categories; laws preserve claims; retrospective lessons organize later memory. None alone can reconstruct unrecorded speech, private grief, informal care, black-market exchange, or the full experiences of civilians.

At 1960, the atlas replaces korea-usa with korea-republic-of over the southern state. The Republic, its people, institutions, disputes, families, infrastructure, and reconstruction continue across that seam. The change corrects a stale hybrid label; it does not record annexation, independence, conquest, collapse, or extinction.

ending.text: At the 1960 snapshot, the exact korea-usa id disappears and korea-republic-of begins. This is a correction of the atlas label and continuity of the Republic of Korea, not a fall, annexation, conquest, independence event, or population replacement. U.S. military government had ended in 1948; the Korean War armistice had halted open fighting in 1953 without a peace treaty; and the April Revolution changed political leadership in 1960 without creating a new state. People, families, schools, workplaces, public-health institutions, infrastructure, disputes, and reconstruction continued. The packet therefore leaves fell null and links the map record directly to the existing South Korea card.
